## Problem and evidence

When an individual customer of a European retail bank is about to buy shares in a US company, such as Coca-Cola, they go through their bank's app. They are not a professional investor. They may have little more than the company's name, its share price or something they read online, and they do not want to spend much time on it. Before placing the order, they want a quick, objective first look at the company, based on figures taken from its annual reports, without reading the full report.

In the United States, companies listed on a stock exchange file an annual report every year (the "10-K"), which is free and accessible to everyone on the SEC website (EDGAR). This report contains the company's complete accounts (balance sheet, income statement, etc.). Yet these reports are rarely downloaded from the SEC website: between 2003 and 2012, a listed company's annual report was requested on average only 28.4 times* by investors right after it was published (Loughran and McDonald, 2017). One of the reasons may be their length: by 2014, they were more than six times longer than in 1995 (Cohen, Malloy and Nguyen, 2020, as summarised by the NBER Digest, November 2018). For a non-professional European investor, it is not realistic to read such a document before each stock purchase, especially since these reports are in English.

\* This figure only includes downloads from the SEC website. Professionals also read these reports via fee-paying terminals.

So, these investors get their information elsewhere and often have limited financial knowledge. Among the youngest, 48% of US Gen Z investors learn about investing mainly through social media (FINRA Foundation and CFA Institute, 2023). In the United States, 26% of investors say they use recommendations from social media influencers when making investment decisions; this rises to 61% of those aged 18–34 and 57% of those with less than two years of investing experience (Lin et al., 2025). On average, US investors answer only 5.3 of 11 questions correctly in an investor knowledge quiz (Lin et al., 2025), and only 18% of EU citizens have a high level of financial literacy (European Commission, 2023). Therefore, many investors make decisions without looking at the company's own figures.

This problem has a real cost. First, it is a cost for the customer. Attention-driven buying can be costly: when users of the Robinhood app (a US brokerage app) buy a stock most heavily on a given day, that stock then has an average abnormal return of −4.7% over the following 20 days (Barber et al., 2022). Moreover, 41% of Gen Z investors in the US and Canada cite fear of missing out as a factor in starting to invest (FINRA Foundation and CFA Institute, 2023). It is also a cost in time: looking for figures and checking information online takes time that not everyone has, especially if their stock portfolio is large. Finally, it is a cost for the bank: it wants to help its customers understand what they buy without giving investment advice, so it needs a neutral tool it can offer next to its order screen.

The customer therefore needs a simple, sourced view of a company's accounts at the moment they buy its shares. Investors also prefer information presented in a visual format, with bullets, charts and graphs (SEC, 2012). The next section presents our solution.

These studies show that the problem exists, not that customers will use Filing Scorecard; most of them describe US investors and some are more than a decade old (see the sources annex).

## Users, market and alternatives

### Who uses it and who pays

| | Who | What they want | What they get |
|---|---|---|---|
| **User** | A customer of a European retail bank who is about to buy shares in a US company | A quick, objective first look at the company before placing the order | A one-page scorecard of pass/fail checks, every number traceable to the company's annual report (see The solution) |
| **Buyer** | The European retail bank that offers the scorecard next to its order screen | To help its customers without giving investment advice | A licensed add-on: a one-off integration fee and an annual licence per bank; customers use it at no extra charge (see Business model) |

**Typical user.** We use France as the example market. In a 2024 survey of active French investors, 67% placed
their orders through a traditional bank, and 47% said they look for information themselves before investing
(AMF, 2024). Problem and evidence describes how much financial knowledge these investors have.

**Why the bank pays.** There is a precedent for a bank's trading platform offering third-party research: in March
2022, AnalytixInsight announced that Morningstar research would be available on InvestoPro, the trading platform
launched by MarketWall and Intesa Sanpaolo (AnalytixInsight, 2022). The announcement does not say who pays for
it, and whether a bank will pay for this particular feature is untested (see Business model).

**Out of scope.** The product covers no banks, insurers or real estate investment trusts (REITs; see The solution).

### How big the market is

Example market: France.

| Indicator | Figure | Source |
|---|---|---|
| French individuals who bought shares in Q2 2025 | 688,000 people, the highest level since 2020 | AMF (2025a) |
| French individuals who bought or sold EU-listed shares in Q2 2025 | 834,000 people | AMF (2025a) |
| French adults who say they are interested in investing in shares | 34% of 2,120 people surveyed (19 September–3 October 2025), the highest since the survey began in 2017 | AMF (2025b) |

**What these figures show.** In France, several hundred thousand individuals bought shares in a single quarter
of 2025, most active investors place their orders through a traditional bank, and the share of adults interested
in shares is the highest since 2017. How many of these investors buy US shares is not known from these sources.

**Market size.** These figures count investors, but the buyer is a bank, so the market is counted in banks:

> Revenue potential = number of banks with an online share-order service × annual licence per bank (€24,000,
> see Business model).

We have not yet counted the European retail banks that offer online share orders, so this plan gives no market
total.

### Alternatives today and how we differ

| Alternative | Cost to the user | What it gives | Its limit for our user |
|---|---|---|---|
| Read the 10-K yourself (SEC EDGAR) | Free | Complete, official figures | Long and technical, and rarely read (see Problem and evidence) |
| Free finance websites | Free | Prices, ratios, news | In our team's own experience, they rarely show which filing a figure comes from |
| Social media and influencers | Free | Opinions | Unchecked (see Problem and evidence) |
| General AI chatbots | Free and paid versions exist (team's own observation) | A written answer on request | Already used: 11% of French adults turn to AI for information before investing, measured for the first time in 2025 (AMF, 2025b). In our team's own experience, an answer does not come with the filing behind each figure |
| Simply Wall St | Free plan with limits; paid Premium and Unlimited plans (prices not shown on its public plans page, checked 24 November 2026) (Simply Wall St, n.d.-a) | Company analysis with a fixed set of pass/fail checks, documented in its public model (Simply Wall St, n.d.-b) | A subscription the user pays for |
| Morningstar Investor | USD 249 a year (US price at launch; the current price may differ) (Morningstar, 2022) | Morningstar research and portfolio tools (Morningstar, 2022) | A subscription the user pays for; our product uses no analyst forecasts (see The solution) |

**How we differ.** Filing Scorecard combines three things: it is free for the user (see Business model), it is shown in
the bank's order screen, and every number links to its filing, reporting line and filing date, with a figure
that cannot be read shown as "not assessed", never guessed (see Systems view and risks). It uses no forecasts and no AI
model when it runs, so the same company always gets the same scorecard (see The solution).

**Limit.** The prototype covers five large US companies. Before submission, six figures of each company are
checked by hand against its 10-K, 30 in all (see Systems view and risks).

<!-- from sections/E-bank-changes.md -->
## How the bank changes

| | Today | With the scorecard |
|---|---|---|
| **Customer** | Does not read the annual reports, which are long and technical; may buy a share because the company is well known, because it is trending, or because of an article seen online. | Sees four areas (past performance, financial health, dividend, valuation) and up to 24 checks, each figure linked to the source it comes from (mostly the annual report), so it can be checked. |
| **Bank** | Has no neutral, sourced view of the company's accounts to offer next to its order screen. | Offers factual information, the same for every customer, without any investment advice. |

Filing Scorecard will change not only what the customer sees but also what the bank must do to provide it. Several teams in the bank must take on new tasks. These roles are derived from our product design (they have not yet been tested in a bank).

- **Data and IT** connects the tool to the bank's own share quote (instead of the price typed by hand in the demo), updates the data, and checks each new annual report.
- **Model validation and risk** reviews the thresholds used by the checks, the tests, and the hand reconciliation of the figures. Because the calculation uses fixed rules and no AI, the same inputs always give the same result, which can be audited.
- **Compliance** confirms that the tool stays information, never advice, and approves showing scores next to the order screen.
- **Advisers and customer service** can explain what the scorecard shows when a customer asks, for example why a check says "not assessed" or why a company shows "no dividend paid".
- **Brokerage** owns the order screen where the scorecard appears.
- **Product owner** decides where and how the tool appears in the app (next to the order screen) and which companies are shown.

So, the customer remains the only one who decides on the investment: the tool will never recommend buying or selling. What changes is that the customer now has a checking step before placing the order. They see which checks the company passes or fails and can trace each figure back to its source, although this does not guarantee a good investment decision.

The bank, for its part, has new decisions to make: which companies to show (only those that have been verified, or others too, labelled "not fully checked"), and how often to update the data. It must also decide how to handle a figure that looks wrong (our product's rule is that a figure is never corrected by hand: the reading rule in the app is corrected, then the app is tested again).

Our aim for the customer is that they understand what they are buying and can check for themselves where every figure they are shown comes from. We aim for all customers to have the same information, whether they are beginners or experienced, at no cost to them.

Our aim for the bank is to be more transparent with its customers, by offering a neutral product that is the same for everyone, and possibly to save its advisers time, which a pilot would need to measure.

A pilot would show whether these aims are met, for example by measuring how many customers open the scorecard before buying, which checks they look at most, and which questions they ask advisers most often.

The tool also has limits. It does not replace investment advice and does not adapt to each customer's needs, so the bank keeps all its usual responsibilities. Banks, insurers and REITs are out of scope, because their accounts are built differently (other limits: see Systems view and risks).

<!-- from sections/A-data-and-controls.md -->
## Systems view and risks

Filing Scorecard gives the customers of a European retail bank (France is our example market) a clearer picture of a company before they place a stock order. It uses 24 checks covering past performance, financial health, dividend and valuation. For the bank, the main question is whether customers can trust the figures and understand their limits. We address this through traceable sources, checks on the calculations and warnings when information is incomplete or outdated.

### What the app depends on

The app uses four main inputs:

| Source | What we use | Freshness and fallback |
|---|---|---|
| SEC EDGAR | Five years of financial figures, share counts and filing dates | Updated when the company files its annual report. Saved copies are available, and the demonstration can run offline. |
| Damodaran’s industry tables | Industry betas, profitability, P/E, P/B and dividend-yield comparisons, plus market benchmarks | Updated each January; we use the January 2026 edition (Damodaran, 2026b). We save the tables with their date, but they can approach a year old between updates. |
| FRED | The ten-year US Treasury rate, averaged over five years for the discount rate | The underlying series is published daily. The app downloads the five-year average when needed and keeps it only in memory, because FRED’s terms require written consent to store its data (FRED, n.d.). If FRED cannot be reached, and in the demonstration, it uses a dated five-year average computed from the US Treasury’s own daily yield-curve rates (US Department of the Treasury, n.d.). |
| Share price | The price used in valuation comparisons | Customers enter it themselves in the prototype. In a bank deployment, it would come from the bank’s quote. |

Saved copies help keep the app available during an outage. However, availability and freshness are different: a calculation can still run using information that no longer reflects current conditions.

Beyond the customers who read the scorecard, a bank deployment involves its brokerage team, which owns the order screen and the quote feed; its IT team, which hosts the app and keeps the saved data current; its compliance team, which approves showing scores beside an order and makes sure they stay information, not advice; and the data providers above. A wrong number or an outdated table therefore reaches customers through the bank’s own channel.

### What can go wrong

The app could select the wrong filing entry, reporting period, unit or sign, or handle a restated figure incorrectly. A company may not report a required figure, and annual reports or industry comparisons may become outdated. External sources can also become unavailable.

There are risks beyond the data itself. The valuation model does not suit every company, customers can mistype a price, and a score shown beside an order screen may be mistaken for investment advice.

The most serious risk is an undetected error that makes a company appear financially stronger or cheaper than it is. Customers may place particular trust in information displayed by their bank, making a misleading result more likely to influence an investment decision.

### How we control these risks

- **Wrong figures:** The sources page identifies the filing, accession number and line item behind each financial input. Accounting checks help identify inconsistencies, including whether assets equal liabilities plus equity within a 1% tolerance.
- **Missing figures:** Missing information stays missing and is never replaced with zero. Checks that require it show “not assessed”, with the reason.
- **Limited verification:** Team members reconciled six figures for each of the five demonstration companies by hand against their annual reports, and all 30 match. Any other ticker displays “not fully checked”.
- **Old information and outages:** Annual reports more than 15 months old display “Latest annual report is old”. Saved industry tables and rate fallbacks retain their dates. For bank deployment, these dates should be clearly visible wherever older inputs affect a result.
- **Unsuitable companies:** The app does not produce an estimate when the cash flow model does not fit.
- **Price errors:** Manual entry remains a weakness of the prototype. Using the bank’s quote and validating any remaining manual entries are proposed controls for deployment.
- **Misinterpretation:** The app avoids trading recommendations and calls its valuation result “the estimate”, never “fair value”. A test keeps advice words such as “buy”, “sell”, “undervalued”, “cheap” and “expensive” out of every check text.

Validation includes more than 1,000 automated tests, 727 cross-checks of figures against an independent route in the same filings for 30 large companies, and an independent spreadsheet model built by a team member (Filing Scorecard team, 2026a).

The app uses no AI internally and no analyst forecasts. Its calculations are repeatable, but they still depend on correct inputs and appropriate assumptions. We built it with AI coding assistants, so we kept people in charge of the numbers: the expected result of every tested calculation comes from a team member’s own hand working or a cited source, never from the code’s output; every change is reviewed by a teammate before it is merged; and our AI-usage log in the repository records where the AI was wrong and how we caught it.

### Limits we admit

The demonstration covers five large US companies, testing has focused on large US companies, and coverage is limited to US filers. Banks, insurers and REITs are outside scope. In this version, industry averages exist only for the industries of the five demonstration companies, so other tickers show “not assessed” for the industry comparisons. Annual reports may miss recent developments, while industry tables can become dated between yearly updates.

The scorecard helps customers understand reported information. It does not remove investment risk or provide investment advice.

<!-- from sections/E-sdg.md -->
## Sustainable Development Goal 9

Seen through SDG 9, Filing Scorecard is a small piece of financial infrastructure: a bank can add it next to its order screen. It aims to make the bank's investment service more accessible, by giving every customer who invests the same analysis for free, and more transparent, because each figure comes from public data and can be checked at its source. The closest target is 9.5, which asks for innovation and stronger technological capabilities; our link to it is indirect, since 9.5 is mainly about research in industrial sectors. Target 8.10 (under Goal 8), on access to financial services for all, is related (United Nations General Assembly, 2017).

These public sources are the audited annual reports that US companies file with the SEC, interest rates from FRED and the industry averages that Professor Damodaran publishes. Since many investors already go through their bank (see Users, market and alternatives), the bank, a domestic financial institution, is well placed to offer this analysis.

However, our contribution to SDG 9 is modest: the tool is a prototype, not research, its impact has not been measured, and the demo covers only five of the thousands of US companies that file a 10-K. As for target 8.10, the tool only helps customers who already have a bank account and can invest, so it does not widen access itself. The pilot described in How the bank changes could measure whether it also reaches less experienced investors, for example through the share of scorecard users who had placed no order in the previous 12 months.

## Business model

### What our demo proves

Filing Scorecard shows how a retail investor could check a company’s accounts before placing an order. In our demo, the customer selects one of five US companies and enters the share price. Someone looking at a dividend can open the check, see the cash paid and follow the link to the annual filing. As of 23 November, the release plan lists 18 checks on past performance, financial health and dividend for the first release and six further checks on valuation for the second. The demo illustrates a workflow a bank could offer beside its order screen using its own share quote. (Filing Scorecard team, 2026b)

A European retail bank is the buyer and its brokerage customers are the users; we use France as the example market. The appeal for the bank is that customers can inspect the evidence behind a score while they are considering a stock. In March 2022, AnalytixInsight announced that Morningstar research would be available on InvestoPro, the trading platform launched by MarketWall and Intesa Sanpaolo. That precedent supports the choice of distribution channel. A bank’s willingness to pay for this particular feature remains untested. (AnalytixInsight, 2022)

### What a bank would need

The five companies in our proof of concept give a bank enough scope to evaluate the workflow. Before a customer rollout, the bank would need a verified list of stocks relevant to its customers, a connection to its own quote feed, production hosting, security testing and compliance approval for displaying scores beside an order. Next steps covers implementation. The following data and licensing conditions affect the business case.

- **Industry benchmarks.** Aswath Damodaran says his published data are openly available and users who acknowledge him as the source need no separate permission from him. Through his NYU affiliation, he has access to S&P Capital IQ and Bloomberg and explains that his providers protect their company-level data. For a commercial rollout, we would budget for a feed whose licence covers the industry figures and company classifications shown to customers. The commercial licence is not priced yet. (Damodaran, 2026a)
- **Treasury rate.** FRED’s general licence is for personal, non-commercial use, and any commercial use needs the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis’s prior written consent (item (j) of its terms). Item (p) of its prohibitions also requires written consent to store or cache FRED content (FRED, n.d.). The design therefore does not cache the download: the app fetches the rate when needed, keeps the five-year average in memory only and falls back to a dated value saved with the app. That value comes from the US Treasury’s own public yield-curve data, not from FRED (US Department of the Treasury, n.d.). For commercial use we would seek FRED’s written clearance or take the rate from a source that permits it (Filing Scorecard team, 2026b).
- **Access to filings.** SEC filing data is public and free to use under the SEC’s fair-access rules. The project limits requests for SEC filings to five per second, below the SEC’s published maximum of ten. (Filing Scorecard team, 2026b; SEC, n.d.)
- **Scoring method.** Simply Wall St licenses its model document, `MODEL.markdown`, under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. “NC” means non-commercial. A paid product would need Simply Wall St’s permission to reuse or adapt the licensed material, or it would need its own independently developed method. (Simply Wall St, n.d.-b)

### Build or buy

In our team’s experience, five finance students built the prototype in about two weeks using AI coding assistants. That makes an in-house prototype a credible option for a bank with engineers supporting its order screen. A production service would also require the verification and approvals described above. When a new annual report appears, someone still has to check that the app picked the right figures, investigate discrepancies and maintain the links customers rely on. When the app misreads a figure, the fix goes into the app’s rules and is tested again; no one overwrites a figure by hand (Filing Scorecard team, 2026b). The bank would own that work under an internal build. We assume one working day to verify each company’s annual filing, or €600 per stock per year. Each additional stock adds that work for an in-house team. A provider serving several banks that cover the same stock could check the filing once and share the cost across those banks. Each bank would still need its own integration and approval.

If the bank buys, we propose a **one-off integration fee plus an annual licence per bank**, with customers using the feature at no extra charge. The licence would cover an agreed set of stocks, filing updates and support. The bank could compare the provider’s offer with its own cost of covering the same companies to the same standard.

### Rough pilot costs and indicative price

We price the pilot in euros for a European bank. The estimate covers one order screen and five companies for a year, assuming the bank supplies its quote feed and production hosting. We use **€600 per working day** as a planning rate, rounded from Malt France’s published **€594/day** average for experienced Python freelancers. Malt does not specify VAT treatment alongside that figure. Our estimates exclude VAT. The days are task-based planning assumptions for a prospective pilot. We have no measured bank integration times. (Malt France, 2026)

| Work | How we estimated it | Supplier cost per pilot |
|---|---|---:|
| Connect and hand over the pilot | 4 days for the quote feed and order screen, 2 for branding, 4 for acceptance testing and handover | €6,000 once |
| Verify and update the data | 1 day per company for its annual filing review, plus 7 days across the year for benchmark updates and discrepancies | €7,200/year |
| Maintain the software and support the bank | An average of half a day per month for fixes and release tests, plus half a day a month for bank questions | €7,200/year |
| Run a supplier test server | One OVHcloud VPS-1 from €3.81/month before VAT with a 12-month commitment paid upfront (€4.49/month without) × 12 months | From €46/year |
| **Total identified costs** | **10 integration days, then 24 working days and one test server per year** | **About €20,450 in year one and €14,450 on renewal** |

The server estimate uses the advertised entry price. The bank would budget its own hosting, security review and staff time separately. (OVHcloud France, 2026)

**Indicative price.** We would charge €6,000 for integration, which covers the ten setup days, and propose an annual licence of €24,000 per bank (€30,000 in year one). The identified recurring costs come to about €14,450 a year. As a planning judgement, we would reserve roughly 40% of the fee because we still need to price data rights, legal and security work, sales and overhead. That leaves 60% for the costs in the table. Dividing €14,450 by 60% gives roughly €24,000. At that price, about €9,550 remains each year to cover those unpriced items before any profit. An extra day of support per month would use €7,200 of that amount, leaving about €2,350. Supplier quotes and measured support time would determine whether the proposed fee is viable.

<!-- from sections/E-next-steps.md -->
## Next steps

For Filing Scorecard to become a real bank product, several steps are needed.

**The product.** The demo covers five companies; a bank would need a verified list of the stocks its customers actually buy, checked again each year when new annual reports are filed. The tool should also assign each company to its industry group automatically: today this is done by hand for the five demo companies, so for any other company seven checks show "not assessed" (the four that compare with the industry, and the three that need the estimate). Two features planned but not built in the prototype could then be added: short texts on each company's strengths and points to watch, and an export of the figures to Excel.

**Integration in the bank.** The tool should use the bank's own share price instead of a price typed by hand. Before customers can use it, the bank needs production hosting, security testing and compliance approval for showing scores next to an order.

**Data rights.** Some free data and the scoring method cannot be used commercially without permission: a commercial rollout would need a data feed licensed for the industry figures shown to customers, FRED's written clearance for the interest rate, and our own documented scoring and valuation method, so that no licensed material is reused (see Business model).

**The pilot.** A pilot with one bank would measure the time needed to integrate and support the tool and collect supplier quotes for the data licences, to test whether the proposed licence of €24,000 a year covers the costs (see Business model). It would also measure how customers use the scorecard (see How the bank changes). The bank could then decide whether to build the tool itself or buy it.

### How the sources support the argument

1. Annual reports are available to everyone but are hardly read (1), partly because they have become very long (2).
2. Retail investors often turn to fast but unchecked sources, especially young and new investors (3a, 3b), and find the documents they receive about their investments less useful than before (3c).
3. Many people lack the financial knowledge to read accounts themselves (4).
4. The bank remains the main channel through which investors place orders (7), and advisers are an important source of information for French adults (5) and investors (6). The bank is therefore well placed to offer a plain, sourced reading of the accounts next to its order screen, without giving advice.

Do not write that investors "trust" the bank most: none of these sources measures trust.

### Limits to state honestly

- Source 1 covers filings from 2003–2012, and only downloads from the SEC website: professionals also read 10-Ks through paid terminals, so 28.4 does not measure all reading.
- Source 2's figure is taken from the NBER Digest summary.
- Source 3c is about documents on investment products, not annual reports.
- Source 5 is a press release, not the full Baromètre. Its figures describe French adults, not investors only, and it does not say whether the shares are of everyone surveyed or of those who invest.
- Sources 4 to 7 describe European and French adults or investors, while the app analyses US companies. This fits a European bank offering US stocks; say so in the text.
